```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.5)
summary_file <- Sys.getenv("EVOMOD2_FE_SUMMARY",
                          system.file("extdata", "fluctuating_environments.rds", package = "evomod2"))
has_results <- nzchar(summary_file) && requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
```

do O & Whitlock (2023, *Evolution Letters* 7: 457-466) simulated populations
whose optimum jumps every few generations, either for all traits together
(correlated change) or for each trait on its own (independent change), with a
genotype-phenotype map that lets pleiotropy evolve: weight genes `a` and a
matrix of contribution genes `C`, `z = C a`. They concluded that

1. correlated change gives more genetic covariance than independent change;
2. most of the difference is pleiotropic, not linkage disequilibrium;
3. block-correlated change (traits 1-2 together, 3-4 together) gives
   modularity;
4. the mutational covariance evolves to match the environment, through the
   epistasis between weight and contribution genes;
5. populations do best in the kind of environment they evolved in.

Their argument rests on pleiotropy being able to evolve. This vignette tests
the claims with four architectures that differ in exactly that:

| Architecture | Pleiotropy | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `contribution_matrix()` | continuous, evolves (their model) | replication |
| `binary_b()` | binary, evolves (Melo & Marroig 2015) | independent test |
| `multilinear()` | fixed pattern; random epistasis makes mutational effects depend on the background | intermediate |
| `additive()` | fixed, isotropic mutational covariance | control |

The simulations run in a few hours of computing, so this vignette shows the
results of a run stored in the package. The script `fluctuating_environments.R`
in `system.file("examples", package = "evomod2")` runs them.

## Setup

The scales follow do O & Whitlock: four traits, 1000 individuals, 5000
generations; every 10 generations the optimum moves by 0.2 up or down, within
[-1, 1]; `omega = I`; no environmental noise; 0.01 mutations per individual per
generation, of standard deviation 0.5 (the value used in their code, which the
paper describes as a variance). The other architectures have 20 loci, like
their 20 genes, and the same mutational input.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(evomod2)
environment <- fluctuating(5000, every = 10, step = 0.2, omega = diag(4),
                           structure = "correlated",   # or "independent", list(1:2, 3:4)
                           bounds = c(-1, 1))
model <- evomod_model(contribution_matrix(traits = 4),
                      contribution_mutation(rate_weight = 0.005 / 8,
                                            rate_contribution = 0.005 / 32, sd = 0.5))
pop <- evolve(model, environment, n = 1000, record_every = 10)
```

Statistics are averaged over the last 500 generations:

* **genetic covariances and correlations** among traits (`g_matrices()`),
  within and between the blocks 1-2 and 3-4;
* their **pleiotropic and linkage disequilibrium parts**, by shuffling alleles
  among individuals (`g_decomposition(method = "shuffle")`), as do O &
  Whitlock did;
* the **mutational covariance**, the covariance of the effects of single new
  mutations in the evolved population (`mutational_covariance()`);
* **fitness in each environment**: the evolved population, with pleiotropy
  frozen (no mutations of `C` or `B`), is moved to each kind of environment for
  2000 generations with an unbounded optimum, and its mean fitness is
  averaged over the last 200.

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = has_results}
library(ggplot2)
res <- readRDS(summary_file)$results
arch_labels <- c(contribution_matrix = "Contribution matrix", binary_b = "Binary B",
                 multilinear = "Multilinear", additive = "Additive")
env_labels <- c(correlated = "Correlated", independent = "Independent", blocks = "Blocks")
res$architecture <- factor(arch_labels[res$architecture], arch_labels)
res$environment <- factor(env_labels[res$environment], env_labels)
n_rep <- max(table(res$architecture, res$environment))
env_colours <- c(Correlated = "#D55E00", Independent = "#0072B2", Blocks = "#009E73")
theme_set(theme_minimal())
mean_ci <- function(d, value, by) {
  a <- aggregate(d[[value]], d[by], function(x)
    c(mean = mean(x), lo = mean(x) - 1.96 * sd(x) / sqrt(length(x)),
      hi = mean(x) + 1.96 * sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))))
  data.frame(a[by], a$x)
}
```

## 1. Correlated change and genetic covariance

```{r, eval = has_results}
d <- mean_ci(res, "G_cor", c("architecture", "environment"))
ggplot(d, aes(environment, mean, colour = environment)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi)) +
  facet_wrap(~ architecture, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = env_colours, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean genetic correlation",
       subtitle = sprintf("Means and 95%% confidence intervals of %d replicates", n_rep)) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

Mean genetic covariance and variance, correlated and independent change:

```{r, eval = has_results}
tab <- aggregate(cbind(G_cov, G_var) ~ architecture + environment,
                 res[res$environment != "Blocks", ], mean)
tab[order(tab$architecture), ]
```

## 2. Pleiotropy or linkage disequilibrium?

```{r, eval = has_results}
parts <- rbind(
  data.frame(res[c("architecture", "environment")], part = "Pleiotropic", value = res$pleio_cov),
  data.frame(res[c("architecture", "environment")], part = "Linkage disequilibrium", value = res$ld_cov))
d <- mean_ci(parts[parts$environment != "Blocks", ], "value", c("architecture", "environment", "part"))
ggplot(d, aes(environment, mean, fill = part)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey50") +
  facet_wrap(~ architecture, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#CC79A7", "#56B4E9"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean genetic covariance") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## 3. Modularity under block-correlated change

Mean genetic correlation within the blocks (traits 1-2, 3-4) and between them:

```{r, eval = has_results}
blocks <- rbind(
  data.frame(res[c("architecture", "environment")], pair = "Within blocks", value = res$G_cor_within),
  data.frame(res[c("architecture", "environment")], pair = "Between blocks", value = res$G_cor_between))
d <- mean_ci(blocks, "value", c("architecture", "environment", "pair"))
ggplot(d, aes(environment, mean, colour = pair)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.4)) +
  facet_wrap(~ architecture, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#E69F00", "grey40"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean genetic correlation") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

## 4. Mutational covariance

Mean correlation between the effects of a new mutation on different traits,
in the evolved populations. In the additive control the mutational covariance
is fixed (isotropic), so this is zero by construction:

```{r, eval = has_results}
d <- mean_ci(res, "M_cor", c("architecture", "environment"))
ggplot(d, aes(environment, mean, colour = environment)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey80") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi)) +
  facet_wrap(~ architecture, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = env_colours, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean mutational correlation") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

## 5. Fitness in each kind of environment

Mean fitness of populations evolved in each environment (rows) when moved to
each environment (columns), with pleiotropy frozen:

```{r, eval = has_results}
fit <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("correlated", "independent", "blocks"), function(test)
  data.frame(res[c("architecture", "environment")], test = env_labels[[test]],
             value = res[[paste0("fitness_", test)]])))
fit$test <- factor(fit$test, env_labels)
d <- mean_ci(fit, "value", c("architecture", "environment", "test"))
ggplot(d, aes(test, mean, colour = environment)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~ architecture, nrow = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = env_colours, name = "Evolved in") +
  labs(x = "Test environment", y = "Mean fitness") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

## What the architectures say

```{r, include = FALSE, eval = has_results}
m <- function(arch, env, v) mean(res[res$architecture == arch & res$environment == env, v])
fit <- function(arch, evolved, test) m(arch, evolved, paste0("fitness_", test))
f2 <- function(x) { x <- round(x, 2); x[x == 0] <- 0; formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2) }
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = has_results}
cat(sprintf("
* **Claims 1-3 hold for every architecture, including the additive control.**
  Correlated change raised the mean genetic correlation from %s to %s in the
  additive model, whose mutational covariance cannot evolve, and from %s to %s
  with the contribution matrix. Block-correlated change made G modular in all
  four (additive: %s within blocks, %s between). In the shuffle decomposition
  the difference is pleiotropic in every architecture, including the additive
  one. There, the pleiotropic part is not a change in how genes affect traits:
  selection sorts alleles, enriching those whose (randomly drawn) effects on
  different traits point the same way, as Jones et al. (2004) described for a
  fixed mutational covariance. So more covariance, modularity and a
  pleiotropic basis of G do not, on their own, show that pleiotropy evolved.

* **Claims 4 and 5 hold only for the contribution matrix.** Its mutational
  correlation followed the environment (%s after correlated change, %s after
  independent change, and %s within blocks against %s between them after
  block-correlated change), and with pleiotropy frozen, populations did best in
  correlated and block-correlated environments if they had evolved in them (in
  correlated environments, %s if they evolved under correlated change against
  %s under independent change); in independent environments, populations from
  all three histories had similar fitness.
  In the binary B model the mutational correlation stayed near %s in every
  environment (alleles affect several traits in the same direction, whatever
  the environment) and populations from different environments had the same
  fitness. In the additive and multilinear models the mutational covariance
  barely changes, and there was no home advantage either.

* The evolution of the mutational covariance, and the lasting advantage it
  gives, needs a developmental map in which the direction of pleiotropic
  effects can evolve continuously, as in do O & Whitlock's model. Genetic
  covariance and modularity in G do not need it.

* Correlated-over-independent covariance ratios (do O & Whitlock report 16-19)
  are not a good measure here: under independent change the mean covariance is
  close to zero, so the ratio is unstable. Differences in correlation are more
  informative.
",
  f2(m("Additive", "Independent", "G_cor")), f2(m("Additive", "Correlated", "G_cor")),
  f2(m("Contribution matrix", "Independent", "G_cor")), f2(m("Contribution matrix", "Correlated", "G_cor")),
  f2(m("Additive", "Blocks", "G_cor_within")), f2(m("Additive", "Blocks", "G_cor_between")),
  f2(m("Contribution matrix", "Correlated", "M_cor")), f2(m("Contribution matrix", "Independent", "M_cor")),
  f2(m("Contribution matrix", "Blocks", "M_cor_within")), f2(m("Contribution matrix", "Blocks", "M_cor_between")),
  f2(fit("Contribution matrix", "Correlated", "correlated")), f2(fit("Contribution matrix", "Independent", "correlated")),
  f2(m("Binary B", "Correlated", "M_cor"))))
```

These runs differ from do O & Whitlock's in the life cycle: evomod2 has
diploid individuals and discrete generations, their model haploid
individuals and overlapping generations (one birth and one death at a time).

## Running it

```sh
script=$(Rscript -e 'cat(system.file("examples", "fluctuating_environments.R", package = "evomod2"))')
Rscript $script simulate contribution_matrix correlated 1 results   # one replicate
Rscript $script summarise results fluctuating_environments.rds
```

Each replicate takes 10-20 seconds; run them in parallel, one per process.
